ch00.note: Xuantong (宣統) was the reign title of Puyi, the last emperor of the Qing dynasty, who came to the throne as a small child in 1908. Its second year corresponds to 1910 and its third to 1911; the dynasty fell in the revolution of 1911–1912, so these are the closing years of imperial China. The novel pairs each reign–year with its Western date, as here.

ch01.note: Bannermen (旗人) were members of the Eight Banners, the hereditary military and social organization of the Manchu Qing dynasty. To call the Rong family Bannermen marks them as part of the ruling Manchu caste—a caste that, in this year of 1911, stood on the very eve of the dynasty’s fall.

Jinlian (金莲) means ‘golden lotus,’ the conventional term for a woman’s bound foot. The name is pointed: this bride has natural, unbound feet (天足), and Master Rong prides himself on opposing foot-binding—so she is a ‘golden lotus’ that was never bound. The lotus embroidered on the muddied shoe in the Prologue belongs to the same motif.

ch01.anchor: withered like a yellow leaf in the west wind
ch01.note: The chapter title, 草木摇落露为霜 (‘grass and trees shed their leaves, and dew turns to frost’), is a line from the Yan ge xing (燕歌行, ‘Song of Yan’) by Cao Pi (187–226), long taken as the earliest complete seven-syllable-line poem in Chinese: the autumn wind is bleak, the weather cold; grass and trees shed their leaves, and dew turns to frost. Its images of autumn decline set the key for a chapter of deaths, a lost child, and a withered wife.

ch02.note: Historically accurate. The Manifesto of the Communist Party was first published in London in February 1848; the 1888 English edition mentioned just below—translated by Samuel Moore and edited by Engels—is likewise real. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen to which Cong Feng compares it was adopted in 1789, during the French Revolution.

Lin Daiyu—and the other names in this passage: Jia Tanchun, Xue Baochai, Shi Xiangyun, Qingwen, Siqi, Xiren, Yuanyang—are all figures in the eighteenth-century novel Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦). Lishui flatters herself with the young ladies’ sensitivity, talent, shrewdness and grace; A-Chu privately assigns her the maidservants’ sharp tongues and pride instead. The whole comparison is lost on a reader who does not know the book.

The chapter title, 朝生春晖暮留霭 (‘born at dawn to spring’s light, wrapped in mist by dusk’), turns on 春晖, ‘spring sunlight’—a classical figure for a mother’s love, from Meng Jiao’s (751–814) Youzi yin (游子吟, ‘Song of the Wandering Son’), which asks how the heart of an inch-long blade of grass can ever repay the light of three spring months. It is Fourth Madam’s maternal hold, not the abstract authority of the Rong house, that binds the wandering A-Chu.

ch03.anchor: sunk in the pond to drown
ch03.note: Chen tang (沉塘), ‘sinking in the pond,’ was a lineage punishment in old rural China: an offender against sexual morality—an adulterer, or a couple who eloped—might be bound and drowned in a village pond on the clan’s authority. Rong Sheng invokes it to measure how far England lies from home.

The source here reads 威尔逊卡迪芙 (‘Wilson Cardiff’). Cardiff is the capital of Wales (威尔士), and 威尔逊 (Wilson) appears to be a slip in the source for 威尔士; it is rendered simply as Cardiff throughout, as elsewhere in the book.

The chapter title, 同林春鸟各自飞 (‘birds of the same wood each take flight’), invokes the folk saying husband and wife are birds of the same wood; when calamity comes, each flies its own way (夫妻本是同林鸟，大难临头各自飞). The chapter scatters its pairs: A-Chu turns back from Cong Hui to save a stranger’s child, and Cong Hui reaches the harbour only to find him already gone.

ch04.note: Juntong (军统) is shorthand for the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Nationalist Military Affairs Commission, the Kuomintang’s secret-police and intelligence service. Strictly, it bore that name only from 1938; in 1931 its institutional forebears were just taking shape, so the term is used a little anachronistically here. The Communist Special Branch (特科) on the other side, however, was real and active in Shanghai from 1927, which fits the novel’s date exactly.

The two codenames are drawn from classical nature-images. Piaofeng (飘风, ‘whirlwind, drifting wind’) echoes the Daodejing: a whirlwind does not last a whole morning. Shiyu (时雨, ‘timely rain’) is the seasonable rain of the classics, falling just when it is needed. Wind and rain, the storm about to break, run all through this chapter’s talk of ‘a storm tonight.’

The chapter title, 阴差阳错难提防 (‘by a cross-grained twist of fate, hard to guard against’), rests on the idiom 阴差阳错—literally a ‘yin-error, yang-mistake,’ a chain of small chances that throws everything awry. The chapter runs on such accidents: a lost admission notice, a stranger’s helping hand, and a crate that proves to be nothing like what it seems.

ch05.note: The chapter title, 时人不识凌云木 (‘the people of the day know not the cloud-piercing tree’), and the couplet Du Luning recites are from the quatrain Xiao song (小松, ‘The Little Pine’) by the late-Tang poet Du Xunhe (杜荀鹤, 846–904): from small a prickly seedling deep in the grass, and now little by little it clears the weeds; the people of the day know not the cloud-piercing tree, till it has pierced the cloud, and then they call it high. Long read as the poet’s self-portrait, it turns on the failure to recognize greatness before it is obvious—exactly Du Luning’s point about the untried Yang Muci. Where the received text reads 直待 (‘wait until’), the novel quotes 直到 (‘until’).

ch05.anchor: Is it not a joy to learn
ch05.note: Du Luning opens with the first lines of the Analects of Confucius (论语 1.1): Is it not a joy to learn and to practice in season what one has learned? Is it not a delight to have friends come from afar? Is he not a gentleman who feels no rancor though others take no note of him? The ‘Sayings of Master Zeng’ he quotes a moment later—each day I examine myself on three points—are Analects 1.4, the words of Confucius’s disciple Zengzi (曾子). That a spymaster should recast the Confucian program of self-cultivation as a lesson in obscurity and infiltration is the passage’s deliberate irony.

‘Director Dai’ is Dai Li (戴笠, 1897–1946), head of the Nationalists’ military-intelligence apparatus and one of the most feared men in Republican China, sometimes called ‘China’s Himmler.’ His formal command of the Juntong dates only from its founding in 1938; naming him here, in a scene set in 1931, is of a piece with the novel’s slightly early use of ‘Juntong’ (see the note at Chapter 4).

ch06.note: Gege (格格) was a Manchu title borne by daughters of the Qing imperial house and higher nobility, roughly ‘princess’ or ‘young lady of rank.’ To nickname He Yashan ‘He Gege’ is to mark her, half in earnest and half in mockery, as a scion of the fallen Qing aristocracy—the ‘old Qing loyalists and their heirs’ (清朝遗老遗少) of the sentence before.

‘Save the children’ (救救孩子) is the famous closing cry of Lu Xun’s A Madman’s Diary (狂人日记, 1918), the founding story of modern Chinese fiction, where it is the diarist’s last hope that a generation not yet made cannibal might still be spared. In He Yashan’s mouth the words carry that literary charge—a plea against a devouring world—beneath their plain surface.

The chapter title, 宫花旋落已成尘 (‘the palace blossom, swiftly fallen, is already dust’), draws on the ‘palace flower’ (宫花) of Tang verse—the blossom in the deserted palace that stands for youth and beauty spent unseen, as in Yuan Zhen’s Xing gong (行宫): lonely, the old traveling-palace; its palace flowers red in silence. The exact line does not appear to be a quotation from any single canonical poem; it works rather as an echo of that whole tradition, bodied out here in the two young lovers cut down and in the fainting girl Rong Sheng sees fall like a flower.

‘The judge of horses had met his thousand-li steed’ renders 伯乐总算遇到了千里马: Bole (伯乐) was the legendary judge of horses of antiquity, and a ‘thousand-li horse’ (千里马) one that could run a thousand li in a day—together a byword for a discerning patron who recognizes rare talent, Du Luning casting himself as Bole to Yang Muci’s steed. In the digital source a stray line of pirate-website advertising (‘阳光中文网 www.sunshe.com…’) is appended to this sentence; it belongs to the file, not the novel, and is kept verbatim in the bilingual record but left out of the reading text.

ch07.note: The chapter title, 却疑春色在邻家 (‘and I half-suspect the spring’s colors are next door’), is the closing line of Yu qing (雨晴, ‘Clearing After Rain’) by the late-Tang poet Wang Jia (王驾): before the rain, first the buds seen among the flowers; after the rain, not a flower left beneath the leaves; the bees and butterflies in a throng go over the wall—and I half-suspect the spring’s colors are next door. Its wistfulness—beauty always just elsewhere, just out of reach—keys a chapter of longings deflected and a homecoming that rings a little hollow. (The widely printed ‘蜂蝶纷纷…却疑’ wording is the version polished by Wang Anshi.)

‘The Old Buddha’ (老佛爷) was the customary honorific for the Empress Dowager Cixi (慈禧, 1835–1908), who dominated the late-Qing court for nearly half a century. Fourth Madam’s unfinished boast—that she once attended the Old Buddha—places her, before her life in the Rong house, among the palace women of the last imperial reigns.

ch07.anchor: the pearls had returned to Hepu
ch07.note: ‘The pearls had returned to Hepu’ renders the idiom 合浦珠还. Hepu (合浦), a southern coastal commandery famous in Han times for its pearl fisheries, was said to have lost its oysters when grasping officials over-harvested them, and to have seen them return only when an upright governor, Meng Chang, restored good rule (Book of the Later Han). Ever since, the phrase has meant the recovery of something precious once lost—here, First Madam’s son restored to her.

ch08.note: The chapter title, 前度杨郎今又来 (‘Young Yang of former days comes again’), reworks the closing line of Liu Yuxi’s (刘禹锡, 772–842) quatrain Revisiting the Xuandu Temple (再游玄都观): the hundred-mu courtyard half moss now, the peach blossom all gone and the rape-flower come; where is he now, the Daoist who planted the peaches? Liu of former days comes again (前度刘郎今又来). Liu wrote it in 828, on returning to the capital after fourteen years’ banishment that an earlier poem on the same temple had provoked—a flourish of unbroken defiance. Swapping 杨 (Yang) for 刘 (Liu) bends that homecoming to A-Chu’s own: the young man of Yang blood coming back, all unknowing, to the Yang house. The attribution is corroborated.

‘A leopard-cat exchanged for the crown prince’ (狸猫换太子) is the celebrated story, popularized by the Qing novel The Three Heroes and Five Gallants (三侠五义) and the opera stage, in which a jealous palace consort has a newborn prince—the future Emperor Renzong of Song—secretly swapped at birth for a skinned wildcat, so that the true heir is cast out and reared in obscurity. Rongrong lets the phrase slip because it fits A-Chu too well: a child of unknown origin in a great house, and, as the reader half-guesses, not the foundling he is taken to be. The tale is legend, not history.

ch08.anchor: the darkest spot right beneath the lamp
ch08.note: ‘The dark beneath the lamp’ (灯下黑) is a common saying: an oil lamp throws its light outward and leaves its own base in shadow, so the spot nearest the flame is the least watched. In tradecraft it is the hiding place in plain sight—here, a hunted man sheltering in the basement of a newspaper office the authorities would never think to search.

ch09.anchor: as though he himself were the dead infant
ch09.note: The chapter title, 开门人即闭门人 (‘the one who opens the door is the one who closed it’), echoes a Chan Buddhist verse attached by legend to the philosopher Wang Yangming (王阳明, 1472–1529): visiting a monastery, he is said to have found a sealed room bearing his own name on a dead monk’s spirit-tablet and the lines fifty years hence, Wang Yangming; open the door and it is still the man who closed it (开门犹是闭门人)—a parable of rebirth, the self returning to a threshold it once shut behind it. A-Chu opening the shrine doors upon the dead child’s altar carries the same charge of one identity crossing the boundary of death. The verse is folk legend rather than documented fact.

‘Gallant of the Crimson Bower’ (怡红公子) is the studio-sobriquet of Jia Baoyu, the pampered hero of Cao Xueqin’s Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦), after his garden apartment the Court of Crimson Joy (怡红院). For the dissolute Tang Shaoli to style himself so is pure self-flattery—claiming Baoyu’s charm while owning only his idleness. (The ‘five poisons,’ 五毒, are the stock vices of the wastrel: feasting, drink, whoring, gambling, and opium.)

The Aisin Gioro (爱新觉罗) were the ruling clan of the Qing dynasty. Aisin means ‘gold’ in Manchu, and after the dynasty fell in 1911 many of the clan took the Han surname Jin (金, ‘gold’)—the sense kept, the Manchu form dropped. A-Chu’s point is that even the emperors’ own kinsmen are commoners now, and Tang Shaoli’s talk of ‘upper sorts’ is an anachronism. Corroborated.

ch10.anchor: cut the flower of one heart by mistake
ch10.note: The chapter title, 误剪同心一片花 (‘by error the flower of one heart is cut’), turns on 同心—the 同心结, or ‘heart-knit knot,’ a looped love-token that Tang poets made a byword for constant love (Chao Cai’s Midnight Songs: . . . and tie it into a heart-knit knot, 绾作同心结), and by extension the 同心花, the twin-lobed ‘flower of one heart.’ To ‘cut’ it by mistake is to sever a bond of joined hearts unawares—A-Chu’s figure for Rong Sheng, who, fleeing his own past, lets a warped affection snip the love that was his. The line is not a traceable single quotation but is built in the classical manner from this love-knot imagery (cf. Li He’s Su Xiaoxiao’s Grave: 无物结同心，烟花不堪剪).

ch10.anchor: hardest of all to nurse oneself through
ch10.note: A-Chu quotes Li Qingzhao (李清照, 1084–c. 1155), the greatest of the Song ci poets: the season when it is warm one moment and cold the next is hardest of all to nurse oneself through (乍暖还寒时候，最难将息), from her Sheng sheng man (声声慢). The lyric is a widow’s lament, and the doctor’s tag—ostensibly mere seasonal counsel—carries for the reader the poem’s undertow of loss, set against the wounded, self-deceiving He Yashu. Corroborated.

The Duke of Windsor was Edward VIII (1894–1972), who in December 1936, less than a year on the British throne, abdicated to marry the twice-divorced American Wallis Simpson—giving up, as A-Chu says, the realm for love. The broad triangular ‘Windsor knot’ is named for him; by most accounts, however, he never tied one, achieving his full-knotted look with specially thick-lined ties knotted four-in-hand. The abdication is corroborated; the knot’s attribution to him is the popular story rather than his own practice.

ch11.anchor: the fortunes of his life, adrift like duckweed
ch11.note: The chapter title, 平生际遇似萍飘 (‘a whole life’s fortunes drift like duckweed’), is the opening line of the fortune-oracle quatrain A-Chu draws at the Ciyun Temple, whose closing line in turn furnishes the title of Chapter 12. It is not a quotation from any single poem but is built in the classical manner on the old image of the duckweed (萍)—rootless, carried wherever the water takes it—for a life at the mercy of chance; compare Wen Tianxiang (文天祥, 1236–1283), Crossing Lingding Yang (过零丁洋): the land is torn like willow-down scattered on the wind, this life afloat and sinking like duckweed beaten by the rain (身世浮沉雨打萍). The whole oracle also foretells the plot: the foundling who has ‘mistaken the strange land for home.’

ch11.anchor: a one-horned beast of legend from high antiquity
ch11.note: A-Chu is unpacking the archaic graph 灋 for 法 (‘law’). The Shuowen jiezi (说文解字, c. 100 CE) defines it: 灋 is punishment; it is level as water, and so takes the water radical; the 廌 is what gores the crooked and drives it away. The 廌 (zhì) is the 獬豸 (xièzhì), a mythical one-horned beast that butts the guilty party in a dispute; from antiquity it was an emblem of justice, its image worn on the caps and robes of the censorate. A-Chu’s gloss is thus exact—and Ronghua’s retort, why then does he not butt, turns the etymology against his own submission. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: Let there be, beside the gate of the grave, young life at play
ch11.note: Rong Sheng quotes the close of Pushkin’s lyric of 1829, Whether I Wander Along Noisy Streets (Брожу ли я вдоль улиц шумных): and let young life play at the entrance of the grave, and let indifferent nature shine on in beauty everlasting. The lines console by setting fresh life against death’s very door—a bleak comfort in the mouth of the jilted Rong Sheng. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: One cannot know the true face of Mount Lu
ch11.note: A-Chu quotes the closing couplet of Su Shi’s (苏轼, 1037–1101) quatrain Written on the Wall of Xilin Temple (题西林壁): one cannot know the true face of Mount Lu, only because one stands within this very mountain. The poem’s point—that whoever is caught inside a thing cannot see its whole shape—is doubly apt for a man who cannot yet read his own origins. (The received text has 只缘, ‘only because’; the novel quotes 只因, of the same sense.) Corroborated.

ch12.anchor: what day shall he go home to wash the traveller's robe
ch12.note: The chapter title, 何日归家洗客袍 (‘what day shall I go home to wash the traveller’s robe?’), is the closing line of the Chapter 11 oracle quatrain, and is lifted verbatim from the ci Yi jian mei: Passing Wujiang by Boat (一剪梅·舟过吴江) by the Song poet Jiang Jie (蒋捷, c. 1245–c. 1305): what day shall I go home to wash the traveller’s robe? Tune the silver-charactered pipes, burn the heart-shaped incense . . . Jiang Jie wrote as a man stranded far from home after the fall of the Song; the ‘traveller’s robe’ carries the wanderer’s ache to return, which here becomes the foundling A-Chu’s own. Corroborated.

ch12.anchor: Pear blossoms fall, apricot blossoms open
ch12.note: The tanci lyric Fourth Madam sings is the aria of Jiao Guiying (敫桂英) from The Ardent Probe (情探), the stage version of the old tale Wang Kui Betrays Guiying (王魁负桂英, out of the Fenxiang ji): abandoned by the scholar she once saved and raised to office, Guiying kills herself and returns as a ghost to reproach him. Her lament—pear blossoms fall, apricot blossoms open . . . I gaze till my eyes break through the autumn waters, and not one letter comes—is sung by that ghost, which is why A-Chu, a moment later, calls the song ‘ghost-talk’ and names Jiao Guiying and The Ardent Probe. The chill he feels is the song’s, and the plot’s.

The Third Communist International, or Comintern (共产国际), was the Moscow-based federation of Communist parties founded by Lenin in 1919; the Chinese Communist Party was affiliated with it from its founding in 1921. For Cong Feng to have ‘gone to the Soviet Union and joined the Third International’ marks him, in the eyes of the Nationalist police of the novel’s Shanghai, as a revolutionary of the most dangerous stripe. Corroborated.

ch13.note: The chapter title, 琵琶声泣血泪仇 (‘the pipa’s cry weeps blood, a feud of tears’), is not a quotation but plays on the long tradition of the pipa as the instrument of lament, crowned by Bai Juyi’s (白居易, 772–846) Song of the Pipa (琵琶行, 816), in which a courtesan’s playing on a river barge moves the whole company to tears: of all who sat there, who wept the most? The Marshal of Jiangzhou—his blue gown wet through. Here the weeping pipa is Fourth Madam’s, and the grief it pours out is a twenty-year blood-feud. An allusion to that tradition, not a direct quotation.

Ximen Qing (西门庆) and Pan Jinlian (潘金莲) are the adulterous pair of the classic novels Water Margin (水浒传) and The Plum in the Golden Vase (金瓶梅): Pan, wife to the meek Wu Da, takes the rich rake Ximen Qing for her lover, and the two poison her husband to be rid of him. They are the standing byword in Chinese for a wife and her paramour who murder the husband—precisely the crime Fourth Madam lays at the door of her uncle and the concubine. Fiction, not history.

A ‘red-capped merchant’ (红顶商人) was a trader who also held official rank—the red button (顶戴) of a Qing mandarin worn atop the merchant’s hat—and so could do business under the protection and licence of the state. The type is epitomized by Hu Xueyan (胡雪岩, 1823–1885), the great financier of the late Qing. To make the murdered father such a merchant, and his wife the daughter of a secret-society chief, sets the family at the very crossing of official wealth and underworld power. Corroborated.

ch14.note: The chapter title, 去时血漫桃源路 (‘when she went, blood ran red on the road to the peach-blossom spring’), turns Tao Yuanming’s (陶渊明, 365–427) famous fable The Record of the Peach Blossom Spring (桃花源记, c. 421) inside out. There a fisherman follows a stream lined with flowering peach trees to a hidden valley whose people, having fled the wars of an earlier age, live in perfect peace, walled off from the world’s strife; 桃源, ‘the peach-blossom source,’ has been the Chinese byword ever since for an untouched refuge. The line makes that refuge run with blood: the hospital where A-Chu meant to take ship for a free life becomes instead a field of slaughter. The allusion is corroborated; the bloody inversion is the novelist’s own.

A-Chu measures himself against a maxim of Mencius (孟子, 4th c. BCE), from Exhausting the Mind I: ‘in want, keep your own self good; come to greatness, and make the whole world good besides’ (穷则独善其身，达则兼善天下). To ‘keep one’s own self good’ (独善其身) is to hold one’s integrity intact when one cannot mend the world; A-Chu’s despair is that even this last, least virtue is now being stripped from him. Corroborated.

ch14.anchor: cut the flesh from his own thigh
ch14.note: The Fourth Madam’s taunt invokes 割股疗亲, ‘cutting the flesh of one’s own thigh to heal a parent’—the extreme of filial devotion, in which a child boils a slice of his own flesh into medicine for a dying elder. A stock motif of the dynastic literature of filial exemplars, it stands here for the doctor (and the son) who will give his own body for those to whom he owes his life; she is saying A-Chu is no such doctor. Corroborated as a traditional motif.

ch14.anchor: wiped out by his very hand
ch14.note: The Chinese (她要自己亲手除去这一对狗男女) is grammatically ambiguous: the reflexive 自己 (‘oneself’) attaches to the sentence’s subject, the Fourth Madam, so the line can be read ‘she wanted to wipe them out with her own hand.’ Yet her whole scheme, stated plainly elsewhere, is that the killing must be done by Yang blood—by A-Chu—while she only looks on; the speech just above says as much (‘I want you to kill them with your own hands’). We render the sense the plot requires and flag the looseness rather than smooth it over.

ch15.anchor: how high the source once lay
ch15.note: The chapter title, 到底方知出处高 (‘only in the end do you know how high the source lies’), is the second line of the poem A-Chu writes back to Rong Sheng on his fan, which reworks a celebrated Tang quatrain on a waterfall, the Linked Verses on the Waterfall (瀑布联句): through a thousand crags and ten thousand ravines it grudges no toil; only seen from afar do you know how high its source lies; how could the brooks and gorges ever hold it back?—in the end it reaches the great sea and becomes the breakers. Tradition makes it a joint work: the opening couplet by a Chan monk, the close by Li Chen (李忱), the future Emperor Xuanzong of Tang (r. 846–859), then living in obscurity. The novel credits the monk as Xiangyan (香严); scholarship more often names Huangbo Xiyun (黄檗希运), with Xiangyan a competing ascription—the poem is genuine and Tang, the monastic attribution disputed. Despite the echoing ‘方知…高,’ this is a different poem from Du Xunhe’s The Little Pine quoted at Chapter 5: A-Chu’s waterfall, unlike the unrecognized pine, already knows its own height and is bound for the sea.

ch15.anchor: fire of sin comes down like thunder
ch15.note: This second passage from the phonograph is the other half of the aria footnoted at Chapter 12—the song of Jiao Guiying (敫桂英) from The Ardent Probe (情探), the stage version of the old tale Wang Kui Betrays Guiying (王魁负桂英). There the courtesan, cast off by the scholar she once raised to office, takes her own life and returns a ghost to drag him across the border of yin and yang and exact the debt of her death (孽火…拉入阴阳界，索还命债). At Chapter 12 the Fourth Madam herself sang the earlier verse, and A-Chu felt a chill run to his marrow; now she lies in the coffin the record plays before, and the song’s wronged, self-slain woman, come back for blood, has been made flesh in her own end. Corroborated.

ch15.anchor: the three knives and the six holes
ch15.note: ‘Three knives and six holes’ (三刀六洞) is a penance of the Jianghu brotherhoods: a member who has broken faith submits to being run through three times, each thrust leaving an entry and an exit wound—three knives, six holes—paying the debt off with his own blood and body. In offering to ‘spare’ Han Zhengqi the three knives and six holes, A-Chu already speaks as the head of the society, holding the old man’s life in his hand. A recognized secret-society usage.

ch16.note: At this point, and again twice at the dinner table below (‘A-Chu set down the silver spoon’; ‘Which company has the Yang family’s bank worked with…’), the source prints 杨慕次 (Yang Muci), the spy-school twin, where the scene is plainly his brother 杨慕初 / 阿初 (Yang Muchu / A-Chu): Muci is away in Hangzhou sitting his final examination throughout this chapter and cannot be in the Shanghai garden or at the Rong dinner table. The twins’ given names differ by a single character (次 / 初), and the slip is almost certainly authorial or typographical; it is rendered here by context (Muchu / A-Chu) and flagged rather than silently reconciled.

ch16.anchor: drove Scholar Zhang out of his wits
ch16.note: Rong Chu is humming a line from The Romance of the Western Chamber (西厢记), the Yuan-dynasty music-drama by Wang Shifu (王实甫, c. 1250–1300): 则为他临去秋波那一转，风魔了张解元. ‘Scholar Zhang’ (张解元) is the student Zhang Sheng (张生), the play’s hero, whom a single parting glance from Cui Yingying leaves lovesick; 解元 is the title of the man placed first in the provincial examinations. The line reworks Zhang’s own famous cry in the first act, 怎当他临去秋波那一转 (‘how could I withstand that one turn of her autumn glance as she went’); Rong Chu sings the paraphrase current in the sung tanci (弹词) storytelling tradition, which Young Tang at once forbids him.

The September 18th Incident (九一八事变), also called the Mukden Incident, of 1931: on the night of 18 September the Kwantung Army staged a bombing on the South Manchuria Railway near Shenyang (Mukden) and used it as a pretext to occupy Manchuria — the ‘Three Eastern Provinces’ (东三省) of Liaoning, Jilin, and Heilongjiang — within months, setting up the puppet state of Manchukuo in 1932. It touched off the nationwide boycott of Japanese goods that is the backdrop to A-Chu’s anger here, and it fixes the chapter’s present after the autumn of 1931, consistent with the 1932 newspaper notices later in the chapter.

ch16.anchor: how does that make a man less a man
ch16.note: A-Chu quotes the second line of Lu Xun’s (鲁迅, 1881–1936) quatrain In Answer to a Guest’s Jest (答客诮): 无情未必真豪杰，怜子如何不丈夫 (‘the heartless are not surely the true heroes; to cherish one’s child — how does that make a man less a man?’). Lu Xun wrote it on 31 December 1932, rebuking those who had mocked his fondness for his infant son; the whole poem is a defense of a father’s tenderness. In A-Chu’s mouth, as he watches the bird’s nest, it turns cold: he has just used that very tenderness — Han Zhengqi’s love for his son Han Yu — as the lever by which to bind the father to him.

The chapter title, 山回路转又逢君 (‘the hills wind, the road turns, and I meet you again’), inverts the closing couplet of Cen Shen’s (岑参, c. 715–770) Song of White Snow, Seeing Off Assistant Magistrate Wu on His Return to the Capital (白雪歌送武判官归京): 山回路转不见君，雪上空留马行处 (‘the hills wind, the road turns, and I see you no more; only the tracks of your horse are left on the snow’), one of the most celebrated farewells in Tang poetry, a parting on a snowbound frontier. Zhang Yong turns Cen Shen’s ‘I see you no more’ (不见君) into ‘I meet you again’ (又逢君): the chapter’s winding mountain roads end not in separation but in Ronghua’s ‘Welcome home’ to Yang Muci, a reunion of comrades in place of a leave-taking. The allusion is corroborated; the couplet is Cen Shen’s, from a poem securely in the Tang canon.

ch17.note: The chapter title, 各有经缝一片天 (‘each has a sky of its own warp and weft’), is not a traceable classical quotation but a couplet in the old manner supplied by the author, and is rendered here literally. 经缝 (jingwei) is the warp and weft of weaving, and by extension the ordering of affairs, the threads by which a scheme is run — the same image Xu Yuzhen turns on Han Zhengqi here (经缝万端, ‘the threads of warp and weft run to a thousand ends’) and which returns when the three antagonists sit down face to face, each ‘nursing designs of his own’ (各怀经缝). The title’s point is that each party to the confrontation weaves a private world of intrigue beneath one shared sky.

The September 18th Incident (九·一八事变), known in the West as the Mukden Incident: on 18 September 1931 officers of Japan’s Kwantung Army staged an explosion on the South Manchuria Railway near Shenyang (Mukden) and used it as a pretext to seize the city and, within months, all of Manchuria. Chiang Kai-shek’s Nationalist government ordered ‘absolute non-resistance,’ and Japan set up the puppet state of Manchukuo the following year. The account here is historically accurate.

Doihara Kenji (土肥原跴二, 1883–1948) was a real Japanese Army officer and spymaster, for decades the chief of Japanese military intelligence in China; after the war the Tokyo tribunal convicted him as a Class-A war criminal and he was hanged in 1948. The likening of women agents to ‘cherry blossoms’ drifting onto the mainland belongs to the novel. The ‘Liyang Society’ (立洋社) and its ‘Eastern Institute’ (东洋学馆) on Kunshan Road are not attested under those names in the historical record and appear to be the book’s invention, though they echo the real use of Japanese-run ‘institutes’ and trading houses in Shanghai as covers for intelligence work.

Lu Yu (陆羽, 733–804), honored as the Sage of Tea (茶圣) for his Classic of Tea (茶经), the first treatise on the subject. The six lines A-Chu recites are Lu Yu’s own Song of Six Longings (六羽歌), one of only two of his poems to survive; the ‘waters of the West River’ and ‘Jingling’ name the river and the town of his childhood home, in present-day Tianmen, Hubei. The quotation is accurate.

ch17.anchor: we sprang, the two of us, from the selfsame root
ch17.note: These four lines are the famous Seven-Step Poem (七步诗) attributed to Cao Zhi (曹植, 192–232). By tradition his brother Cao Pi, the new emperor, ordered him to compose a poem in the time it took to walk seven paces, on pain of death, and Cao Zhi answered with these lines on beans boiled over a fire of their own stalks — brother destroying brother though both are of one root. A-Chu quotes it for plain reason: the whole book turns on twin brothers set against each other, and on kin who murder kin.

ch17.anchor: ran a deliberately strange, sidelong gaze over her
ch17.note: Here, and here only in this chapter, the source prints 杨慕次 (Yang Muci), the spy-school twin, where the speaker is plainly his brother 杨慕初 / 阿初 (Yang Muchu / A-Chu): the whole tearoom confrontation is A-Chu’s, and he has given his own name as Yang Muchu only a few lines above. The twins’ names differ by a single character (次 / 初), and the slip — recurring from the previous chapter — is almost certainly authorial or typographical; it is rendered here by context and flagged rather than silently reconciled. The familiar name 阿次 / A-Ci, by contrast, is genuinely Muci’s.

ch18.anchor: out of the tangled and disordered threads
ch18.note: The chapter title, 牵丝攀藤一条线 (‘drawing the silk, climbing the vine, a single thread’), plays on the set phrase 牵丝攀藤, to drag in far-fetched or tenuous connections. The phrase is ordinarily disparaging (‘pulling east and attaching west’), but the title turns it to A-Chu’s method in this chapter, in which he draws every stray, tenuous clue together into one continuous thread of deduction. It is not a classical quotation but a couplet in the old manner supplied by the author, and is rendered here literally.

ch19.anchor: a row of last plum trees
ch19.note: The chapter title, 梅花一夜漏春工 (‘in a single night the plum blossom betrays spring’s craft’), is not a traceable classical quotation but a seven-character line in the old manner supplied by the author, and is rendered here literally. It works within a long poetic tradition—widened by Wang Anshi (王安石)—in which the early plum ‘leaks’ or ‘betrays’ (漏, 漏泄) the news of a spring not yet arrived. The image fits the chapter: in one night A-Chu’s long-hidden self begins to show through—Xin Lili and Cong Feng each take him for his twin, and the Comintern delegate is quietly brought in—as the plum gives away the coming season before its time.

Yu Xuanji (鱼玄机, c. 844–871) was a celebrated Tang-dynasty woman poet, famous for her beauty and her verse and long remembered as a courtesan-poet; A-Chu cites her to argue that a woman of the ‘blue houses’ need not be a wanton. Historically she entered a Daoist convent, not the ‘Buddhist gate’ the source names here (遁入佛门), so that detail is contradicted by the record, though the figure herself is real. 艳帜高张, rendered ‘flew her gaudy flag as high as any,’ means to be renowned as a great beauty.

The 月份牌 (‘calendar poster’) was a form of commercial art peculiar to Republican-era Shanghai: an advertising calendar printed by color lithography, typically showing a fashionable modern beauty or a dapper young gentleman, given away by companies to promote their wares. To liken Cong Feng to a figure on one is to call him decorative and a little unreal.

ch20.anchor: the smile of friends long parted and met again
ch20.note: The chapter title, 一笑相逢哪易得 (‘a meeting met with a smile is not easily won’), is a seven-character line in the old manner supplied by the author, rendered here literally; it is not a traceable single classical quotation, though the phrase 一笑相逢 (‘to meet with a single smile’) is a stock one in Song lyric, as in Zhou Bangyan’s (周邦彦) Die lian hua: ‘一笑相逢蓬海路’. The chapter turns on two such hard-won meetings—the reunion of A-Chu and his old friend Cong Feng, and the first face-to-face of the estranged twins.

A-Chu is needling Cong Feng about where he has really come from. 大海啊，你这自由的元素 renders the apostrophe to the sea in Pushkin’s To the Sea (‘K moryu,’ 1824), commonly Englished ‘Farewell, free element!’; a few lines on, ‘the insulted and the injured’ (被侮辱与损害的) is the title of Dostoevsky’s novel of 1861. Both are Russian touchstones A-Chu drops to signal, under Ronghua’s ear, that the delegate comes from the Soviet Union.

ch20.anchor: There is no water that does not run downward
ch20.note: A-Ci is quoting Mencius (孟子, Gaozi I): 人无有不善，水无有不下—‘there is no man who is not good, and no water that does not run downward,’ the classic argument that human nature is innately good, as water naturally flows down. He turns it on A-Chu to insist there must be some good reason behind the extortion.

Here, and in the dialogue that follows, the source prints the borrowed name in quotation marks, ‘杨羽柏’ (‘Yang Yubo’), and then reverts to the man’s true name, 杨羽桦 (Yang Yuhua). They are one and the same person in the novel’s present: Yang Yuhua, the Yang family’s second master, murdered his elder brother—the real Yang Yubo, Muci’s father—and, being alike in looks, took over his identity, his wealth and his wife (revealed in Chapters 12 to 14). He is rendered here by context and the doubling flagged, not silently reconciled.

ch21.anchor: a bolt from a clear sky
ch21.note: The chapter title, 千钧一发箭在弦 (‘a thousandweight on a hair, the arrow on the string’), gathers two classical figures for a danger poised to break at a touch. 千钧一发 is from Han Yu (韩愈), Letter to Meng Jian (与孟尚书书): 其危如一发引千钧, ‘the peril of it, as a single hair drawing a thousand jun.’ 箭在弦上 is from Chen Lin (陈琳), whose words survive as 矢在弦上，不得不发, ‘the arrow on the string cannot but be loosed.’ Both are corroborated. The novel’s own title, 一触即发 (‘one touch and it goes off,’ said first of a drawn bow—hence On a Hair Trigger), is the same image; and it is here, with the Party’s whole network suddenly poised to fall into enemy hands, that the tension is drawn to its fullest.

老向 (‘Old Xiang’), and below 向先生 / 向书记 (‘Mr. Xiang’ / ‘Secretary Xiang’), are the underground cover-name of Fang Zhitong (方致同), Secretary of the Central Special Branch: comrades address him as Xiang, and so do his captors. All refer to the same man, named in full by the narration as Fang Zhitong.

ch22.anchor: blocking the vital artery to Hengji Li
ch22.note: The chapter title, 截断众流大气魄 (‘to dam all the currents takes a vast resolve’), turns on the Chan phrase 截断众流 (‘cut off the myriad streams’), one of the ‘three phrases of Yunmen’ (云门三句) attributed to the Tang–Song Chan master Yunmen Wenyan (云门文偃): the other two are 涵盖乾坤 and 随波逐流. As a complete seven-character line the title is not a traceable quotation but the author’s own pastiche in the old manner (like the titles of Chapters 17, 19 and 20); the borrowed Chan figure of ‘damming every stream’ is fitted to Ronghua’s act, which literally dams the flow of both traffic and comrades pouring toward the trap.

ch22.anchor: Gu Shunzhang was a member of the Party's Central Committee
ch22.note: Gu Shunzhang (顾顺章, 1904–1935) really was the head of the Communist Special Branch’s security and ‘Red Squad’ (红队) and a Central Committee member. Arrested in Wuhan in April 1931, he defected at once, threatening to destroy the whole Shanghai underground. The catastrophe was averted because Qian Zhuangfei (钱壮飞), a Communist mole inside the Nationalists’ own cipher office, intercepted the warning telegrams and got word to the leadership, which relocated its organs overnight—exactly the ‘one coded telegram, and in a single night the Communists vanished’ that Adjutant Liu describes. The account here is corroborated by the historical record.

ch22.anchor: Wu Hao—the highest man in charge
ch22.note: ‘Mr. Wu’ / Wu Hao (伍豪) is a documented alias of Zhou Enlai (周恩来), who in this period directed the Communist Party’s Special Branch (特科) in Shanghai. The pseudonym is corroborated; it became notorious in 1932 through the forged ‘Wu Hao notices’ (伍豪启事) planted in the Shanghai press to announce his supposed defection. That the amah expects ‘Mr. Wu’ in person marks how close the raid comes to the very top of the apparatus.

The source here writes 荣华书店 (‘Ronghua Bookstore,’ after its proprietor), whereas everywhere else—including the next chapter—the same shop is named 华美书店, the Huamei Bookstore. The inconsistency is the author’s; both name the one shop, and it is rendered here as the text stands rather than silently reconciled.

ch23.anchor: the very grass and trees seemed to stink of blood
ch23.note: The chapter title, 恶氛弥天血火焚 (‘a foul miasma fills the sky; blood and fire consume’), is the author’s own seven-character line rather than a traceable quotation, rendered here literally. 草木皆腥 (‘even the grass and trees smell of blood’) plays on the set phrase 草木皆兵 (‘every bush and tree looks like an enemy soldier’), from the rout at the Fei River (淝水之战, 383) recorded in the Book of Jin (晋书): the author swaps 兵 (‘soldiers’) for 腥 (‘the reek of blood’) to fit the carnage of the crash.

Rh-negative blood is genuinely rare among Han Chinese—on the order of three in a thousand, as the text says (千分之三), against roughly fifteen in a hundred among people of European descent—so a shared Rh-negative type A is a strong, if not conclusive, sign of kinship. The novel uses it as the physical proof of what the twins do not yet openly acknowledge: it is A-Chu’s stored plasma that saves A-Ci, and the mingling of their blood that first stirs A-Chu’s sense of a brother.

ch24.anchor: a grieving wind fills the road
ch24.note: The chapter title, 风雨未肯收余寒 (‘the wind and rain will not yet give up the lingering cold’), is the author’s own line in the classical manner rather than a traceable quotation; the figure of a late cold that will not lift echoes the stock poetic 余寒 (‘lingering cold’) of early-spring verse. It is rendered here literally. A-Chu’s coded message—悲风满路, ‘a grieving wind fills the road’—carries the same weather into the warning he sends A-Ci.

‘Daiyu burns her manuscripts’ (黛玉焚稿) is the celebrated episode in Chapter 97 of Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦): Lin Daiyu (林黛玉), betrayed in love and dying, burns the poems and handkerchiefs that hold her heart. The First Madam’s remark is corroborated as an allusion to that scene, and doubles as a grim foreshadowing—Ronghua is said to have inherited not only Daiyu’s gifts but her ill-starred, early-cut fate.

ch24.anchor: better to kill a thousand by mistake than let one slip through
ch24.note: 宁可错杀一千，也不放过一个 (‘better to kill a thousand by mistake than let one slip through’), with its cruder twin 宁枉勿纵 (‘wrong the innocent rather than let the guilty go’), is the notorious slogan of the Nationalist ‘White Terror’ that followed the anti-Communist purge of 1927. It is genuinely documented as a watchword of that repression, though its exact origin is disputed and it is only traditionally—not verifiably—put in Chiang Kai-shek’s own mouth; Yu Xiaojiang here cites it as the Generalissimo’s standing instruction.

ch25.anchor: to step backward was, all along, to go forward
ch25.note: The chapter title, 退步原来是向前 (‘to step backward was, all along, to go forward’), is the closing line of the 《插秧诗》 (‘Rice-Planting Song’), a Chan quatrain attributed to the Cloth-Bag Monk (布袋和尚), Qici (契此), traditionally placed in the Five Dynasties. The received text runs 手把青秧插满田，低头便见水中天，六根清净方为道，退步原来是向前 (‘green shoots in hand, he fills the paddy field; head bowed, he sees the sky within the water; only when the six senses are pure is it the Way; to step back was, all along, to go forward’). A-Chu quotes it almost verbatim, though the novel gives a variant third line (顺其自然方是道, ‘to go along with nature is the Way’) and misplaces it in the ‘former Tang.’ The attribution to Budai is corroborated as the traditional one, the poem being among the best known of Chan verses.

ch25.anchor: grafting of one flower upon another
ch25.note: 移花接木 (‘to graft one flower onto another tree’) is a set phrase for a covert substitution, swapping the true for the false so that no seam shows. Here it names A-Chu and Xia Yuechun’s ruse: a look-alike is presented as the injured Yang Muci first, so that Li Qinhong’s men, having fixed his identity by sight, never think to scrutinize the real man’s voice.

ch25.anchor: what the ear hears is empty; what the eye sees is real
ch25.note: 耳听为虚，眼见为实 (‘what the ear hears is empty; what the eye sees is real’) is a common proverb asserting the primacy of sight over hearsay. Xia Yuechun turns it into the very principle of the deception: because the visual cue has already answered the question, his listeners discount the auditory one—precisely the blind spot the substitution exploits.

ch26.anchor: In advancing, no joy; in retreating, no grief
ch26.note: A-Chu’s answer, 进亦不喜，退亦不忧 (‘in advancing, no joy; in retreating, no grief’), inverts the famous antithesis of Fan Zhongyan’s 《岳阳楼记》 (‘Record of the Yueyang Tower,’ 1046), 是进亦忧，退亦忧 (‘thus he grieves whether he advances or retreats’), and echoes its 不以物喜，不以己悲 (‘he takes no joy in outward things, no sorrow in himself’). The allusion is corroborated; A-Chu recasts Fan’s selfless statesman as a portrait of a woman’s equanimity, and hears it, rightly, as a likeness of Yashu.

ch26.anchor: Bai Yun was Tian Xiuyun's alias
ch26.note: The chapter title, 白云可杀不可留 (‘the white cloud may be slain but not detained’), is the author’s own seven-character line in the classical manner rather than a traceable quotation; no earlier source has been found for it (uncorroborated). It puns on 白云, at once the ‘white cloud,’ that drifting emblem of a free and unfettered spirit, and Bai Yun, the alias of the courier Tian Xiuyun, whose old recantation surfaces here to mark her, in the organization’s eyes, for death.

ch26.anchor: you wear out iron shoes tramping in search of it
ch26.note: 踏破铁鞋无觅处，得来全不费功夫 (‘you wear out iron shoes tramping in search of it, and then find it without the least effort’) is a well-known proverb—current from the Southern Song writer Xia Yuanding (夏元鼎) and made familiar by its use in 《水浒传》 (Water Margin)—for a thing long sought in vain that turns up by chance. It is corroborated as an attested saying. Here it marks A-Chu’s stumbling, at the Police Bureau, upon the very voice he has hunted.

ch27.anchor: the roaming fish went to meet death without flinching
ch27.note: The chapter title, 踏破冰火九重天 (‘treading through ice and fire, the ninefold heaven’), is the author’s own line in the classical manner rather than a traceable quotation (uncorroborated); 九重天, the ‘ninefold heaven,’ is the highest of the nine tiers of heaven in old Chinese cosmology. The image of passing through ice and fire answers the chapter’s converging perils—a killing at the Police Bureau, Cong Feng walking knowingly into the trap—gathered here in the figure of the roaming fish that goes to meet death without flinching.

ch27.anchor: the peony of Luoyang is first under heaven
ch27.note: Yang Sitong retells a beloved legend: Empress Wu Zetian (武则天, r. 690–705), drunk on a winter night, decreed that every flower bloom by morning; all obeyed but the peony, which would not, and was banished to Luoyang, where it bloomed the more gloriously—whence the saying 洛阳牡丹甲天下 (‘the peony of Luoyang is first under heaven’). The tale is corroborated as a widely told legend (the ‘scorched-boned peony,’ 焦骨牡丹), though it is folklore rather than official history; Wu Zetian’s own fondness for the Luoyang peony is, however, historically attested. Sitong presses it into service to prove that the peony, for all its opulence, has a ‘proud spine’ (傲骨).

ch27.anchor: turn back, and the shore is there
ch27.note: The two men fence in proverbs. Muci’s 回头是岸 (‘turn back, and the shore is there’) is the latter half of the Buddhist admonition 苦海无边，回头是岸 (‘the sea of suffering has no bound; turn back and there is the shore’), a call to repent while there is yet time. Rong Chu returns 水到渠成 (‘when the water comes, the channel forms of itself’), the saying that conditions ripen of their own accord—a serene refusal to turn back.

ch28.note: The chapter title, 间不容发生死际 (‘not a hair’s breadth between, at the very verge of life and death’), turns on the idiom 间不容发, literally ‘the gap will not admit a single hair.’ It is documented in Mei Cheng’s (枚乘) 上书谏吴王 of the Western Han, where a thread bearing a vast weight over an abyss is described — 系绝于天不可复结，坠入深渊难以复出，其出不出，间不容发 — the margin between rescue and ruin narrower than a hair (corroborated). It is the sister image to the 千钧一发 of Han Yu noted at Chapter 21; here the knife-edge is the instant Yu Xiaojiang’s silenced shot decides who lives.

On 18 September 1931 the Japanese Kwantung Army detonated a charge on the South Manchuria Railway near Liutiaohu, outside Shenyang (Mukden), blamed Chinese troops, and used the pretext to overrun the city and, within months, the whole Northeast — the 九一八 or Mukden Incident (corroborated). The puppet state of Manchukuo (伪满) was proclaimed in March 1932. Yu Xiaojiang’s survey of the war dates the scene to the aftermath of these events.

ch28.anchor: A Short History of Chinese Philosophy
ch28.note: The recognition password names Feng Youlan’s (冯友兰) A Short History of Chinese Philosophy, which the Macmillan Company did publish — but in 1948, more than fifteen years after this scene. The book and publisher are real (corroborated); the date makes the reference an anachronism, the author’s rather than the characters’. Here it serves only as the Party’s fallback contact phrase, to be used if anything befell Ronghua.

ch28.anchor: The kite whose string had snapped was joined to its line again
ch28.note: In the source this sentence is followed by a pirate-site watermark line (阳光中文网 www.sunshe.com…), an advertising string injected by the site that scraped the text and no part of the novel. It is kept verbatim in the bilingual QC file but omitted from the reading text, as with the watermark at Chapter 6.

ch29.note: The chapter title, 欲披荒草访疑尘 (‘wishing to part the wild grass to seek out the doubtful dust’), is a seven-character line in the classical manner that traces to no single documented source; like several titles in this book (Chapters 17, 19, 20, 22, 23, 24, 26, 27) it appears to be the author’s own pastiche (uncorroborated). Its wild grass and doubtful dust answer the brothers’ nocturnal survey of the overgrown, long-shunned Ciyun Temple.

ch29.anchor: The China League for Civil Rights
ch29.note: The 中国民权保障同盟 (China League for Civil Rights) was founded in Shanghai in December 1932, led by Song Qingling, Cai Yuanpei and Yang Quan, and campaigned for the release of political prisoners and the safeguarding of civil liberties (corroborated) — which fixes the chapter to its stated ‘winter of 1932.’ Yang Quan was assassinated by Nationalist agents in June 1933, after which the League effectively dissolved.

Wang Jingwei (汪精卫), a senior Nationalist leader, is associated with the slogan of 曲线救国 / 救亡, ‘national salvation by a roundabout path’ — the argument that accommodation with Japan might buy time and preserve the state. It became the byword for his later collaboration: in 1940 he headed a Japanese-sponsored government at Nanjing (corroborated). Du Luning’s sympathy for it marks him, in the novel, as a man already drifting toward the enemy.

ch30.anchor: To die together is a bond well met
ch30.note: The chapter title, 同生共死亲兄弟 (‘brothers, kin in life and death alike’), is a plain seven-character line in the old manner rather than a traceable single quotation (uncorroborated). It is answered by the twins’ exchange in the flooded crypt, 有缘共死，不枉同生 — a bond that turns their forced descent into the trap into the moment they become, in fact as in blood, brothers.

ch30.anchor: when the false is taken for the true, the true becomes false as well
ch30.note: A-Chu quotes 假作真时真亦假, the first line of the couplet inscribed over the Land of Illusion (太虚幻境) in the Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦, first noted at Chapter 24); its companion line runs 无为有处有还无, ‘where nothing is made something, the something turns to nothing.’ The couplet’s theme of the true and the false changing places is the engine of this chapter’s buried-identity plot (corroborated).

A 名古屋带 (Nagoya obi) is a lighter, partly pre-folded kimono sash. It is in fact a modern invention, devised in Nagoya around 1920 (which contradicts the source’s tying of it to the 桃山 / Momoyama age of the late sixteenth century; the author uses ‘Momoyama’ loosely for ‘old Japanese’). The bright tubular sash is the detail from A-Chu’s recovered childhood memory that fixes the murderer as a Japanese woman.

ch31.anchor: the hook that will never let go
ch31.note: The chapter title, 游鱼见食不见钩 (‘the roaming fish sees the bait, not the hook’), shapes into a seven-character line the old proverb 人见利而不见害，鱼见食而不见钩 (‘man sees the gain and not the harm; the fish sees the bait and not the hook’), a saying against the greed that blinds one to the trap, current in Qing fiction (it appears in the Jing hua yuan, 镜花缘) and traced back to the Guiguzi (鬼谷子). Corroborated as a proverb, though the exact seven-character form is the author’s own. The whole chapter turns on the figure: A-Chu’s ‘fragrant bait,’ the hook he means to sharpen, and He Yashu’s closing reversal — that she is the hook, and it is he who has bitten.

ch32.anchor: rich wine, a fair woman, the mandarin-duck swords
ch32.note: The chapter title, 醇酒美人鸳鸯剑, fuses two allusions. 醇酒美人 (‘rich wine and a fair woman’) derives from the Records of the Grand Historian (史记, Biography of the Lord of Xinling): dismissed from command, the Lord of Xinling (信陵君) drowned his ruin in strong drink and women (饮醇酒，多近妇女) until it killed him — hence ‘wine and women’ as the road of self-destruction. 鸳鸯剑 (‘the mandarin-duck swords’) are the twin-bladed betrothal sword of the Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦), one blade graven 鸳 and its mate 鸯: given by Liu Xianglian to You Sanjie (尤三姐), who cut her own throat with it to prove her honor — the mandarin duck being the emblem of faithful lovers, so the blade stands for love pledged and love turned to death. Both corroborated; the title welds the wine-and-women of a man’s undoing to the lovers’ blade, apt for Koyama Eiko’s seduction of Yang Yuhua and its long, murderous issue.

The anecdote is Plato’s, from the Theaetetus (174a): Thales (泰利士), gazing up at the stars, fell into a well, and a witty Thracian serving-girl laughed that he was so eager to know the heavens he could not see what lay at his feet. Xia Yuechun invokes it by way of coded warning — that A-Chu, intent on the enemy far off, has overlooked the danger at his own side. Corroborated.

ch32.anchor: the deeper its roots reach down into the darkness
ch32.note: A paraphrase of Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Part I, ‘The Tree on the Mountainside’: ‘it is the same with man as with the tree. The more he seeks to rise into the height and light, the more vigorously do his roots struggle earthward, downward, into the dark and deep — into evil.’ Corroborated. Yang Yuhua takes it as licence for his own descent.

ch32.anchor: It is just because life is short that it seems beautiful
ch32.note: In the source this line of dialogue is followed on the same paragraph by a pirate-site watermark (‘阳光中文网 www.sunshe.com…’), an artefact of the digital text and no part of the novel; it is preserved verbatim in the bilingual QC file but dropped from the reading text. The like was noted at Chapters 6 and 28.

ch32.anchor: On the Distinction of the Three Realms of Civilized and Barbarous
ch32.note: 《文野三界之别》, attributed in the text (at Chapter 33) to Liang Qichao (梁启超, 1873–1929), the reformist thinker. The schema of ‘three realms’ of civilization — the savage (野蛮), the half-opened (半开化), and the civilized (文明) — is indeed Liang’s, set out in his Book of Freedom (自由书) and adapted from Fukuzawa Yukichi’s Outline of a Theory of Civilization. Corroborated as Liang’s idea; that A-Chu should keep such a title on his shelves marks him, to Rong Sheng’s eye later, as no ordinary man.

ch33.anchor: the false holding truth, the true holding falsehood
ch33.note: The chapter title, 假做真时真亦假 (‘when the false is made true, the true too turns false’), is the first line of the couplet over the Land of Illusion (太虚幻境) in the Dream of the Red Chamber, already annotated at Chapter 30 (the standard text reads 假作真时真亦假; this chapter uses the variant 做 for 作). Here the theme is literal: the hypnotist’s craft of mingling true memory with false, and the whole chain of stolen identities the chapter unknots.

ch33.anchor: The Eighteen Nao Songs: Shang Ye
ch33.note: 铙歌十八曲·上邪. ‘Shang Ye’ (上邪, ‘O Heaven!’) is a Han yuefu from the eighteen ‘Nao songs’ (铙歌, drum-and-fife pieces of the 鼓吹曲辞): a woman’s oath of undying love, swearing that only when the hills flatten, the rivers run dry, and thunder sounds in winter snow will she part from her lover. Corroborated. He Yashu’s marking of the passage, and her sending the book to A-Chu, is her own such oath.

ch33.anchor: Snow drifts and drifts on Fuji's peak; half of this scene belongs to Edo
ch33.note: A-Chu recites the couplet in Japanese to unmask the false Amah A-Yue: the river-plum snow scene embroidered on his shoes resembles the view from the summit of Mount Fuji, and Edo (江户) is the old name of Tokyo, where he has guessed she was raised. 五分 renders idiomatically as ‘half’ (five parts in ten). The lines are the author’s pastiche in the classical Japanese manner rather than a traceable poem (uncorroborated).

ch34.anchor: turned the guest into the host
ch34.note: The chapter title, 反客为主 (‘turn the guest into the host’), is No. 30 of the classical Thirty-Six Stratagems (三十六计): to arrive as a guest and by degrees seize the position of host and master. Here Muci, coming to his brother’s table and his brother’s operation, drugs A-Chu and takes over the endgame against Yang Yuhua, making the stratagem literal; 深造次, ‘a deep rashness,’ names the presumption of it, and 造次 (‘rash, hasty’) sounds again when Xia Yuechun warns Muci not to act rashly.

百川丛惠子, the captured impostor’s true name. As with her fellow agents Koyama Eiko (小山缨子) and Koyama Chino (小山千野), the surname is read in the Japanese manner: 百川 = Momokawa, an attested Japanese surname, and 惠子 is the common given name Keiko. The middle graph 丛 has no settled kana reading, so the whole romanization is provisional. She is a Japanese agent, and not the real Amah A-Yue (岳嬷嬷), whom she murdered twenty years before in order to take her place.

ch34.anchor: the Land Survey Department of the Army General Staff
ch34.note: 陆军测量部参谋本部. The Land Survey Department (陸地測量部) of the Imperial Japanese Army General Staff was the real body charged with military mapping and survey from 1888 to 1945; the covert surveying of Chinese terrain that runs through Keiko’s confession, and the ‘street maps of Shanghai’ found beneath the shrine hall, answer to its actual work. The novel folds its seduction-and-espionage program into this genuine institution (corroborated).

ch35.anchor: Brothers are like geese in flight
ch35.note: The chapter title, 一举锄奸雁归行 (‘at a single stroke the traitor is rooted out, the wild geese return to their rank’), is the author’s own seven-character line in the classical manner rather than a traceable quotation. 雁行, the ordered flight-line of migrating geese, is an old figure for brothers; the closing chapter turns on the two brothers, long divided, at last taking their places side by side, and Young Tang and Yuechun press the same image (兄弟如雁行) to reconcile them.

ch35.anchor: an order given at dawn is answered by dusk
ch35.note: The broadcast the brothers hear is a real wartime statement of the Chinese National Government under Chiang Kai-shek, issued around the fall of Shanghai in November 1937 (in part: 各地战士，闻义赴难，朝命夕至，其在前线以血肉之躯，筑成壕堑，有死无退…实足以昭示民族独立之精神，奠定中华复兴之基础). It is quoted, corroborated, though the exact document and date are given variously in the sources. The passage frames the novel’s close on the eve of the eight-year War of Resistance.

爱中 (Aizhong) and 爱华 (Aihua), the twins’ infant sons, born December 1933. Both names mean, in effect, ‘love China’ (中 and 华 are each names for the country); read together they spell 爱中华, ‘love China.’ The naming lands pointedly four years before the 1937 invasion with which the book ends.

ch35.anchor: May you cherish the one before your eyes
ch35.note: In the linked verse the four friends cap in turn, the line 愿君怜取眼前人 (‘may you cherish the one before your eyes’) echoes the close of Yan Shu’s (晏殊, 991–1055) song-lyric to the tune Huanxi sha: 满目山河空念远，落花风雨更伤春，不如怜取眼前人 (‘a whole land in the eye, and longing for the far away is vain… better to cherish the one before your eyes’). The point is A-Chu’s: he burns the letter from his old love abroad and turns to Yashu, present and living.
